questions.q: `cargo build -p goose-cli --bin goose` builds:
options: Only the goose-cli package and only its goose binary target
Every workspace member in release mode
Only dependencies of goose-cli, not the crate itself
The goose library plus all binaries in goose-cli
explanation: -p narrows to one package; nothing implies --release, and other members are untouched.
cargo builds the requested crate AND its dependencies, never deps alone.
--bin selects a single binary target; adding a lib would need explicit naming.

questions.q: `resolver = "2"` in the root Cargo.toml selects:
options: Edition-2021 feature unification (dev-dependency features don't leak into the normal build)
Two parallel compilations of the workspace
HTTP/2 for registry downloads
A second Cargo.lock for CI
explanation: The resolver doesn't compile twice.
Transport choice is separate from the feature resolver.
Lockfile count is not a resolver setting.

questions.q: Which tool switches the active Rust toolchain version?
options: rustup
cargo
rustc
clippy
explanation: cargo follows whichever toolchain rustup activated.
rustc is the compiler binary itself.
clippy lints within the active toolchain; it doesn't manage versions.

questions.q: `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` makes warnings:
options: Hard errors — the precommit gate fails on any warning
Silently ignored
Written into a report file
Downgraded to allow
explanation: -D promotes lints; it never silences them.
clippy output goes to the terminal/build, not a designated file.
allow would need an -A flag and works in the opposite direction.

questions.q: `let mut func_token_count = 0;` later used with `+= FUNC_INIT` where `FUNC_INIT: usize = 7;`. The inferred type is:
options: usize, because the += with a usize binds the type
i32, because literals default that way
u8, the smallest type that fits
Undetermined until runtime
explanation: The i32 default only applies without a stronger signal.
Rust never auto-narrows to the smallest type.
Inference is fully compile-time.

questions.q: `let borrowed: &str = "goose"; let owned: String = String::from("goose");` — the key difference:
options: owned allocates and owns its buffer; borrowed points at data owned by something else (here, the binary)
borrowed is shorter so faster to compare
owned cannot be passed to functions
borrowed is mutable, owned is not
explanation: The difference is ownership, not speed of comparison.
String is passed to functions constantly.
Actually the reverse: String can grow, &str cannot.

questions.q: In `fn f() -> usize { let x = 4; x }`, the value 4 is returned because:
options: The block's last expression is the function's return value
let-statements return their bindings
Rust implicitly inserts return;
usize values are auto-wrapped in Result
explanation: Statements produce no value.
No implicit return exists — the expression position is what returns.
Result wrapping is never automatic.

questions.q: `for i in 0..3` prints:
options: Nothing — ranges aren't iterable
explanation: .. is exclusive of the end bound.
The range starts at its left bound, 0.
Ranges are the idiomatic for-loop driver.

questions.q: A match over an enum with 4 variants handling only 3 produces:
options: E0004 non-exhaustive patterns, naming the variant not covered
A runtime error when the 4th variant occurs
A silent default fallback
A clippy-only warning
explanation: The compiler rejects it before runtime.
No fallback exists unless you write `_ => ...`.
It's a hard compile error (E0004), not a lint suggestion.

questions.q: `RetryResult::MaxAttemptsReached(msg)` stores a `msg`. Matching it to use the data requires:
options: Binding in the pattern: `RetryResult::MaxAttemptsReached(msg) => use(msg)`
Calling `msg()` on the variant first
Converting the variant to a Message via as
Accessing it as a tuple index .0
explanation: No accessor exists unless written; binding is the mechanism.
as-casts apply to references/primitives, not enum payload extraction.
Tuple-index access works only for tuple variants if you destructure, not on the enum itself.

questions.q: `let s = String::from("x"); let t = s; println!("{}", s);` gives:
options: E0382 use of moved value — assignment moved ownership to t
It prints x because String is Copy
E0507 cannot move out of borrowed content
A runtime panic
explanation: String owns a heap buffer; it's not Copy.
Nothing is borrowed here; the move is by value.
Moves of owned values are legal — the error is at the use-after-move.

questions.q: A `&mut T` borrow of a value forbids:
options: Any other borrow (& or &mut) of the same value while it lives
Reading the value through the mutable reference
Passing the value to functions entirely
All future borrows forever
explanation: &mut supports reads too — it's exclusive, not write-only.
You can pass through the single &mut; concurrent ones are forbidden.
Later borrows are fine once the &mut ends.

questions.q: `fn trim_prompt(prompt: &str) -> &str` needs no lifetime annotations because:
options: Elision: one input reference means the output borrow is assumed to come from it
The return is 'static
trim() copies the string
Lifetimes are only checked for structs
explanation: No 'static is involved; the link is input-to-output.
trim returns a view, not a copy.
Borrowing functions are checked too — elision just fills in the obvious lifetime.

questions.q: `ModelConfig::new("gpt-4o")` calls an associated function because:
options: It has no self parameter — it's called on the type, not an instance
It's declared outside any impl block
It returns a reference
Associated functions must take String arguments
explanation: Associated functions live inside impl blocks.
new returns Self (an owned value).
Argument types are unrelated to the fn-vs-method split.

questions.q: `let n = limit.ok_or("missing")?;` when `limit: Option<usize>` and the enclosing fn returns `Result<_, String>` does:
options: Binds n to the usize, or early-returns Err("missing") from the fn
Panics on None
Loops until Some appears
Converts None to 0 and continues
explanation: Panic comes from unwrap/expect, not ?.
No retry semantics exist.
None becomes the Err branch, never a fabricated value.

questions.q: `pub trait Provider: Send + Sync` (base.rs:464) declares:
options: Supertrait bounds every implementor must satisfy
Provider's two required methods
That the trait is async
The crate the trait belongs to
explanation: Methods are declared inside the body; bounds follow the colon.
Async-ness comes from #[async_trait] and async fn, not these bounds.
Crate paths appear in use statements, not trait heads.

questions.q: Chaining `?` through several functions gives callers:
options: Each function's context layered onto the underlying error as it flows upward
Only the outermost error, inner causes erased
A guaranteed stack trace
Panics at the first failure
explanation: anyhow keeps the chain; each layer adds context without dropping the cause.
Stack traces need backtrace features and aren't collected by ?.
? returns errors; it never unwinds via panic.

questions.q: A goose app function typically returns:
options: anyhow::Result<T> so any fallible step can use ?
ProviderError directly
A tuple (T, Option<Error>)
Future<T> with side-channel errors
explanation: ProviderError is the library crate's typed enum; app code uses the open-ended anyhow error.
Errors-in-tuples is not the Rust convention.
Failures belong in Result, not side channels.

questions.q: `#[derive(Error)]` plus `#[error("Rate limit exceeded: {details}")]` on a variant generates:
options: Display and Error impls from the template — the variant can be returned as an error
Retry loops keyed on the message
A serde schema for the error
Automatic logs on construction
explanation: Behavior like retries is written by callers, not generated.
Serde derives are separate (Serialize/Deserialize).
Logging requires explicit tracing calls.

questions.q: `#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]` on Message changes:
options: The JSON keys for the struct's fields (and back on deserialize)
The struct's type name to camelCase
String values inside the struct
The memory layout of the struct
explanation: Type names need named renames, not rename_all.
Content values are never rewritten by key renames.
Serde attributes change wire format, not layout.

questions.q: Adding a new field with `#[serde(default)]` keeps old JSON files loading because:
options: Missing keys fall back to the type's Default rather than erroring
Old files are rewritten to include the key
The field is skipped in both directions
All parse errors are suppressed
explanation: Serde never modifies input documents.
skip hides a field; default fills a missing one.
Only that field's absence is tolerated; other errors still surface.

questions.q: An `async fn` body compiles to:
options: A pollable state machine suspended at .await points without blocking the thread
A blocking call until the future completes
A generator object you must drive with next()
A promise polyfill
explanation: Futures poll lazily; awaiting is non-blocking for the runtime thread.
next() drives Streams; a plain future is awaited.
Rust futures are native; no polyfill involved.

questions.q: `#[tokio::main]` on `async fn main` does:
options: Builds the tokio runtime and drives main to completion on its worker threads
Adds retry-on-panic to main
Turns main into a background thread
Enables std Mutex to work across awaits
explanation: No automatic retry exists.
main runs on the runtime's threads, not a detached background one.
std Mutex compatibility with await is a Send question, unrelated to the macro.

questions.q: A MutexGuard releases the lock when:
options: Dropped — normally at the end of its scope
Another lock() call is made
Explicitly told to via unlock() — Rust guards have no such method
The Mutex is Cloned
explanation: A second lock() waits; it can't release the first guard — unlock() doesn't exist, drop is the mechanism.
RAII drop, not method calls, releases locks.
Mutex isn't Clone; even if it were, cloning wouldn't unlock.

questions.q: Holding a std MutexGuard across an .await in goose-style code fails because:
options: The future stops being Send, violating MessageStream's + Send bound
Tokio deletes locks on suspension
The guard's value type changes at the await
Mutexes are forbidden in async crates
explanation: Locks aren't deleted; the Send trait is what's checked.
Guard types are stable across awaits — Send-ness is the issue.
Mutexes are used in async code, just never held across awaits.

miniLab.title: Echo agent: struct + trait + anyhow + serde + async stream + lock-guarded state
miniLab.instructions:
Build a tiny 'echo agent' crate from scratch (this is the capstone of Unit 0 — the unit's exam mini-lab).

1. In your working folder: `cargo new u0-echo-agent`, then `cd u0-echo-agent`.
2. Add deps: `cargo add tokio --features macros,rt,time`, `cargo add futures`, `cargo add async-trait`, `cargo add anyhow`, `cargo add serde --features derive`, `cargo add serde_json`.
3. In `src/main.rs` write all of the following (each maps to a lesson):
   - a serde struct `EchoConfig { model: String, temperature: f32 }` with `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]` (l14)
   - `struct EchoAgent { config: EchoConfig, calls: Arc<Mutex<HashMap<String, usize>>> }` — lock-guarded shared state (l15)
   - a trait with one method, e.g. `trait Agent { async fn stream(&self, input: &str) -> anyhow::Result<StreamOfStrings>; }` implemented with `#[async_trait]` (l12 + l13)
   - in the impl, log the call under `calls` (lock, increment, drop the guard BEFORE any await — l15's golden rule), then build a stream with `futures::stream::unfold` that sleeps ~20ms between pieces (tokio) and yields 2-3 chunks that echo the input plus a `[call N]` counter read from the snapshot (l15)
   - `#[tokio::main] async fn main` that constructs the agent, runs TWO concurrent stream() calls via `tokio::join!`, prints each combined output, and prints `ECHO-AGENT-OK` at the end (l15)
   - define `StreamOfStrings` as `Pin<Box<dyn Stream<Item = anyhow::Result<String>> + Send>>` yourself (l12)
4. Run `cargo run` until you see both streams echo and `ECHO-AGENT-OK` prints.
5. From the folder that CONTAINS the `u0-echo-agent` directory, run the verify script below and paste its full output into the exam answer box:

```powershell
powershell -File u0-echo-agent-verify.ps1
```

Save the verify script's output — the grader checks it contains `VERIFY PASSED` plus the concrete fragments listed in the pass markers.
